def: Includes fixed manufacturing overhead in the cost of each unit.
Assets = Liabilities + Equity, the identity that every double entry preserves.
The older set of Indian accounting standards, which apply to companies not covered by Ind AS.
Revenues and expenses are recorded when earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid.
Income earned in the period but not yet received.
A group of tasks tied to a cost object, such as scheduling, set-ups, purchasing or inspection.
Allocates overhead to products according to the activities that cause it.
The cost actually incurred, compared with the standard.
Debt disciplines managers through fixed payments, at the price of monitoring costs and conflicts with lenders.
The angle at which the sales line cuts the total cost line at break-even; a wide angle means profit builds fast.
A long-term outflow that uses funds, such as buying assets, repaying loans or paying dividends.
Net sales divided by total assets; the sales earned from each rupee of assets.
A statement of what a business owns, owes and has put in by its owners on a single date.
A standard fixed for a base year and not revised.
A costing method for goods made in distinct lots.
An activity done once per batch, such as ordering, set-ups or inspecting a lot.
The study of how psychological biases influence financial decisions.
A measure of how much a share’s return moves with the market.
Selling a bill to a bank before it is due, at a discount.
Funds raised from outsiders, repayable with interest.
A graph of sales and costs showing the level of activity where there is no profit or loss.
The sales level at which contribution equals fixed costs, so there is no profit and no loss.
Continually comparing actual results with budgets, finding variances and acting on them.
Preparing a quantitative financial plan for a period.
The business is treated as separate from its owner, so the owner’s private affairs stay out of its books.
Estimates the cost of equity as the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium.
Evaluating long-term investment projects using tools such as NPV, IRR and payback.
The long-term funds in the business: debt plus equity, or fixed assets plus working capital.
Funds carrying a fixed interest or dividend divided by equity funds.
The mix of debt and equity a firm uses to fund itself.
A forecast of cash receipts and payments to manage liquidity.
Short-term, highly liquid investments that convert readily into known amounts of cash with little risk.
A statement of cash and cash equivalents received and paid, classified into operating, investing and financing.
Cash and cash equivalents divided by current liabilities; the strictest liquidity test.
A short-term unsecured promissory note issued by large firms.
A statement with each item shown as a percentage of sales or total assets, to spot changes.
A ratio with one figure from the statement of profit and loss and the other from the balance sheet, such as debtors turnover.
Provide for expected losses at once, but recognise profits only when realised.
The same accounting methods are used from year to year so results can be compared.
A costing method for large, long projects such as construction.
Sales less variable cost; what each sale adds towards fixed costs and profit.
Recording, classifying, analysing and controlling costs to find unit cost and support decisions.
Assets are recorded at what was paid for them, whatever they later become worth.
The factor that causes the cost of an activity, such as the number of set-ups.
The cost of an activity pool divided by the number of driver units.
Anything for which a separate measure of cost is wanted, such as a product, service, project or customer.
The minimum return a firm must earn to satisfy those who supply its funds.
Interest after tax divided by net proceeds: I(1 − T) ÷ NP.
The return equity holders expect, estimated by dividend growth, earnings yield or CAPM.
Preference dividend divided by net proceeds.
The opportunity cost of keeping profits, taken as about equal to the cost of equity.
A group of indirect costs with similar behaviour, one for each activity.
A statement that builds up cost stage by stage from prime cost to selling price.
A unit of product, service or time for which cost is stated, such as a kilowatt-hour.
Studies how cost, volume and profit move together.
Net credit purchases divided by average payables; how quickly suppliers are paid.
A current asset or liability, such as stock, debtors, cash or creditors.
Current assets divided by current liabilities; a liquidity test with a conventional benchmark of about 2:1.
A standard for present conditions, set for a short period and widely used for control.
Long-term borrowing at a fixed rate of interest; holders are creditors, not owners.
Total debt divided by total assets; the share of assets financed by debt.
Total debt divided by shareholders’ equity; a measure of financial leverage.
Net credit sales divided by average receivables; how quickly customers pay.
The spreading of an asset’s cost over its useful life; it uses no cash and sets none aside.
A cost that can be traced to a specific product or job.
Shows cash received from customers and cash paid out, to arrive at cash from operations.
All material information, including contingent liabilities, must be disclosed fully.
The decision on how much profit to pay out and how much to retain.
Every transaction has two effects, a debit and an equal credit, so Assets = Liabilities + Equity always holds.
A cost driver based on the time an activity takes, such as set-up hours.
Net profit divided by the number of shares.
Ownership shares with voting rights and a dividend that varies with profit.
A forecast of what a cost will be, usually from past data; unlike a standard, it is not a yardstick of efficiency.
A standard that reflects what is expected to be reached in the period ahead.
The out-of-pocket cost of raising funds, such as interest or dividends.
Selling receivables to a financial institution for immediate cash.
The trouble a firm faces when it cannot meet its debts, with costs such as lost customers and forced sales.
Using borrowed money to magnify returns to owners, and the risk with them.
Planning, raising, using and controlling a firm’s funds.
Activities that change the size and make-up of owners’ capital and borrowings.
Net sales divided by net fixed assets; sales produced by each rupee of fixed assets.
A budget that does not change whatever the level of activity.
A cost that stays the same whatever the output, such as rent.
The difference between standard and actual fixed overhead, split into expenditure and volume.
A budget recalculated for the actual level of activity.
A change in working capital, arising only when a current and a non-current account are both affected.
A statement of the sources and applications of funds, where funds means working capital.
Profit adjusted for non-fund items such as depreciation; the main internal source of funds.
The business is assumed to continue, which is why assets are depreciated rather than valued for sale.
Gross profit as a percentage of net sales.
Buying an asset by instalments, with ownership passing after the last one.
Investors borrowing for themselves to copy the effect of a firm’s debt.
A standard set for the best possible conditions, with no waste or idle time.
The opportunity cost of using funds, such as earnings kept back.
India’s accounting standards, converged with IFRS; they apply to companies in notified classes.
A cost that cannot be traced to one product and is shared among products.
Starts with profit and adjusts for non-cash items and changes in working capital.
A cost driver that charges directly for the resources used each time an activity is done.
Earnings before interest and tax divided by interest; how many times interest is covered.
The tax saved because interest is deductible.
The discount rate at which a project’s NPV is zero.
Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory; how many times stock is sold and replaced.
Buying and selling long-term assets and investments that are not cash equivalents.
A costing method for customised, one-off orders.
The first record of a transaction, written in date order with its debit and credit.
The limiting factor, often sales, that decides which budget is prepared first.
Standard labour cost for the actual output less the actual cost; rate, efficiency and idle-time parts.
Standard rate times the difference between standard hours and hours actually worked.
Idle hours times the standard rate; always adverse.
Hours paid times the difference between standard and actual wage rate.
Using an asset for rent without owning it.
A running account to which journal entries are posted, grouped by head such as cash or sales.
Financing mix does not affect value in a perfect market, because investors can lever or unlever themselves.
Adding all the costs of a product or asset from its first idea to its disposal, usually discounted.
Actual sales less break-even sales; how far sales can fall before a loss.
The extra cost of one more unit of output, which is its variable cost.
Sales − Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit.
The cost of raising the next increment of capital.
Treats only variable costs as product costs; fixed costs are charged to the period.
Firms issue equity when they think it is overvalued and avoid it when undervalued.
A consolidation of all functional budgets, with a projected profit and loss account and balance sheet.
Expenses are set against the revenue they helped earn in the same period.
Standard cost of material for the actual output less the actual cost; the sum of price and usage variances.
The part of usage variance due to using materials in a different proportion from the standard.
Actual quantity times the difference between standard and actual price.
Standard price times the difference between standard and actual quantity.
The part of usage variance due to actual output differing from the output the input should give.
Only items large enough to affect users’ decisions need detailed treatment.
In a perfect market with no taxes, a firm’s value does not depend on its capital structure.
The cost of equity rises with leverage: Ke = Ko + (Ko − Kd) × D/E.
Only events that can be expressed in money are recorded in the books.
Holds that more debt lowers the overall cost of capital and raises value.
Holds that the overall cost of capital and value do not change with the debt-equity mix.
Discounted future cash inflows less the initial outlay; accept a project if positive.
Net profit as a percentage of net sales.
A transaction that uses no cash, such as buying a machine by issuing shares; left out of the statement.
A long-term account, such as share capital, reserves, long-term loans or fixed assets.
A standard based on the average of past results.
Explanatory disclosures with the statements, covering accounting policies, contingent liabilities and the detail behind figures.
The firm’s principal revenue-producing activities and other activities that are not investing or financing.
Operating profit as a percentage of sales; the operating ratio’s complement.
Cost of goods sold plus operating expenses, as a percentage of sales.
A cost already incurred but not yet paid, added to the year’s expenses and shown as a liability.
Recovered overhead less actual overhead; the sum of the variable and fixed overhead variances.
Indirect costs of production, administration and selling that cannot be traced to a unit.
Funds provided by the owners; permanent, with no obligation to repay.
Contribution as a percentage of sales; also called the profit-volume ratio.
The time taken for a project’s cash inflows to recover its initial outlay.
Firms prefer internal funds, then debt, and new equity last.
The business’s continuing life is divided into periods, usually a year, for reporting.
Shares with a fixed dividend and priority over equity, usually without voting rights.
A cost paid in advance for a later period, taken out of this year’s expenses and shown as an asset.
Share price divided by earnings per share; the rupees investors pay for each rupee of earnings.
Direct material plus direct labour plus direct expenses.
A costing method for continuous, uniform production such as cement.
Tracing the costs and revenues of a product from research and design to withdrawal from the market.
Units to be made: sales plus closing stock less opening stock.
The aim of increasing profit, usually over a short period.
Estimating the cost of owning a physical asset from purchase to disposal; also called whole-life costing.
Shareholders’ funds divided by total assets; the share of assets paid for by owners.
An amount charged against profit for a known or likely loss or liability whose size is uncertain.
Money accepted from the public for a fixed term at interest, often unsecured.
The materials to be bought: material needed plus closing stock less opening stock.
Current assets less inventory, divided by current liabilities; benchmark about 1:1.
Studying relationships between items in the financial statements to judge performance and position.
Revenue is recognised when it is earned, usually on sale, not necessarily when cash arrives.
Profit kept back in the business; unlike a provision, it is not a charge against profit.
Dividends are paid only from profit left after all acceptable projects are funded.
Profits kept in the business instead of being paid out as dividends.
Net profit as a percentage of total assets.
Profit before interest and tax as a percentage of capital employed; also called return on investment.
Net profit as a percentage of shareholders’ equity.
Identifying financial risks and reducing them through hedging, insurance and diversification.
An estimate of sales in quantity and value; usually the first budget drawn up.
Actual quantity sold times the difference between actual and standard selling price.
Actual sales less budgeted sales; the sum of the price and volume variances.
Standard price times the difference between actual and budgeted quantity sold.
The layout the Companies Act prescribes for a company’s balance sheet and statement of profit and loss.

term: Schedule of Changes in Working Capital
def: A table of each current item over two years showing how working capital rose or fell.
A cost with both a fixed and a variable part, such as an electricity bill.
A long-term inflow that raises working capital, such as new shares, loans, asset sales or operating profit.
A one-off order priced below the usual price; accepted if it adds contribution and does not harm regular sales.
The predetermined cost of a unit under efficient working conditions.
Compares predetermined costs with actual costs to find variances and act on their causes.
A statement showing how owners’ funds moved over the period: profit, share issues, dividends and reserves.
A statement of income, expenses and the resulting profit or loss for a period.
Closing stock divided by working capital.
Depreciation of the same amount every year: depreciable amount divided by useful life.
Total assets divided by long-term debt; how many times assets cover the debt.
Buying from suppliers now and paying later.
Firms balance the tax benefit of debt against the costs of financial distress.
A cost driver that counts how many times an activity is done, such as orders or inspections.
A list of ledger balances that checks total debits equal total credits before statements are drawn.
Using the same cost methods across several firms or units so costs can be compared.
A cost that changes in proportion to output, such as raw materials.
Another name for marginal costing; only variable costs are charged to products.
The difference between standard and actual variable overhead, split into expenditure and efficiency.
The difference between standard and actual cost, favourable if actual is lower and adverse if higher.
The aim of increasing the value of the firm over time, allowing for the timing and risk of cash flows.
The average cost of all sources of finance, weighted by their share of total capital.
Arranging year-end figures, such as paying creditors early, to make ratios look better.
Current assets less current liabilities; the money tied up in day-to-day running.
Depreciation at a fixed percentage of the asset’s reducing book value each year.
Every item of spending must be justified afresh, with no assumption that last year’s costs continue.
